title: Kausalya's blessing
hookLine: his mother is praying for his coronation when he walks in to tell her

lines: AND HE HAS TO TELL HER.
cards: Kausalya has been up since before dawn, dressed in white silk by the sacred fire, making offerings for her son's success. She's waited years for this morning.

Valmiki tells us she's long been the least favored of the king's wives, and today was going to change that. Then Rama comes in. She's so glad to see him she rises to bless him, and offers him a seat and something to eat.
And he has to tell her.

teach.b: Rama tells her gently, and she collapses. When she can speak, her grief pours out. If I'd had no son at all, she says, I'd have had one sorrow.
Now I have this. She's ready to follow him into the forest. Lakshmana is in the room too, furious; we'll come back to his anger in a few days.
Today, watch Rama. He doesn't raise his voice, and he doesn't change his mind.

He reminds her of others who obeyed a father's word at great cost, and one example is startling: Parashurama, the sage with the axe we met on the road, who once obeyed his father even against his own mother.
Then Rama turns to Kausalya's own path. Your place is with the king, he says. He's old and grieving.
Stay with him. Slowly she steadies, and the scene turns. Kausalya stops arguing and starts blessing.
She calls on the gods, the seasons, the rivers, the mountains, the days and nights, to protect her son wherever he goes.
Valmiki gives her blessing at length, and she ties a protective charm on his arm, the way Hindu mothers and grandmothers still bless a child before a journey.

Here's the thread back to the Ramayana's first verses, where Valmiki asks Narada: who in the world has mastered himself, ātmavān ko jitakrodho, who has conquered anger? Jitakrodha. Today we see what it looks like.
Not a man without feelings, but a son who holds his mother's grief, his brother's rage and his own loss in one room, and stays kind.

how: Blessing a child before a journey or a rite, often with a sacred thread tied on the wrist, is still common in Hindu families; in the text, Kausalya blesses Rama at length and ties a protective charm on his arm before he leaves.

o: a cold distance he keeps from his weeping mother
steadiness that holds others' grief without anger
the silence of a son who won't say goodbye

games.q: the mother's room — tap the pairs.
p: praying by the fire in white silk
Kausalya ties it on Rama's arm

s: Kausalya accepts the exile at once
she collapses and wants to follow him; only slowly does she turn to blessing.
the question about conquering anger is from the Ramayana's first verses
it's part of what Valmiki asks Narada.
Rama tells his mother to come to the forest
he asks her to stay with the grieving king.

games.q: you're Rama. your mother wants to come with you into exile. what do you say?
o: stay with the king; he's old and grieving.
games.why: Rama tells her that her place is with his father. she steadies, and blesses him at length.

practice: Picture someone close to you who's upset right now, about anything; you don't need to fix it. On each breath in, feel a little of what they feel; on each breath out, send them steadiness, the way Rama did for his mother.
If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Rama's calm, with his mother. He holds Kausalya's grief steadily until her grief turns to blessing: jitakrodha, one who has conquered anger.

orig.note: Sanskrit jitakrodha: one who has conquered anger, jita (conquered) plus krodha (anger). Valmiki asks after such a person in the epic's first verses.

carryVoice: Your line: jitakrodha: anger conquered, kindness kept. Tomorrow, the question of blame. That's day five hundred twenty-four.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 20–21 (Kausalya's grief; Rama's answer; the example of Parashurama)
